summary: PlayCanvas is two things under one name: an open-source runtime released under the MIT licence, and a hosted editor and publishing service at playcanvas.com. The runtime is a mature real-time renderer on WebGL 2 and WebGPU, with an entity-and-component scene model, glTF 2.0 reading and writing, animation state graphs, positioned sound, WebXR sessions, and unusually deep support for Gaussian splats including level-of-detail streaming. Physics is not in the runtime: rigid bodies, collision shapes, joints and trigger volumes ship as components that stay inert until the application separately loads ammo.js, a WebAssembly port of Bullet. The runtime carries no networking, no identity, no persistence and no avatar model at all, and PlayCanvas documents multi-user work only as tutorials that wire a scene to a third-party server such as Socket.io, Colyseus or Photon. The first trap for a standards audience is the product split: reading FBX or COLLADA, baking font atlases, compressing textures, resolving template overrides and producing a runnable package are all hosted-editor jobs done on PlayCanvas servers, and none of them exist in the open-source runtime. The second trap is that several load-bearing conventions, including right-handed axes with Y up, column-major matrices and one unit to the metre, are stated in source comments or a single documentation page rather than specified anywhere normative.

coverage.note: The runtime has its own frame graph of render passes driving a forward renderer with clustered lighting and an ordered layer composition; there is no deferred path.

coverage.note: No rights or licence metadata is carried on an asset; the glTF copyright field is never read on import and never written on export, and asset tags are only a search aid.
Nothing is signed. The only authorship field touched is the glTF generator string, which the exporter writes as plain unverified text.
There is no avatar format. An avatar is an ordinary glTF mesh like any other model, and there is no VRM support anywhere in the repository or the documentation.
Bone names come from whatever the source file used; PlayCanvas defines no naming or structure convention, so nothing guarantees a rig transfers.
Morph targets provide the mechanism for facial shapes, but there is no named set of expressions or visemes, so nothing survives a move between worlds.

There is no retargeting anywhere in the runtime; animation curves bind to entity paths by name, so a clip plays on another body only when the two hierarchies happen to use identical names, and nothing maps or rescales bones.
Items can be parented to a bone using the ordinary scene hierarchy, but there is no attachment-point definition that would survive transfer to another world.
No avatar level of detail, and no mesh level of detail to build it on.
A rendering runtime with no avatar model and no identity layer has nothing to bind.

Static, dynamic and kinematic bodies are provided by a rigid-body component that ships in the runtime but does nothing until the application or project separately loads ammo.js, a browser port of Bullet that is deliberately not bundled because of its size.

sources.title: Real Time Multiplayer | PlayCanvas Developer Site

coverage.note: No notion of ownership or authority over an object exists, because there is no shared state to own.
No interest management. Whatever a chosen third-party server does is outside PlayCanvas.
No prediction or reconciliation helpers; the tutorials leave latency hiding entirely to the application.
The runtime ships only an HTTP request helper. There is no session transport, no web socket layer and no wire protocol of its own.
No live audio or video transport. Video can be shown as a texture from a browser element, but nothing carries streams between participants.
There is no concept of joining a running world and no end-user authentication; the accounts on playcanvas.com belong to developers, not to the people who visit a published application.
Nothing carries state from one world to another. Moving between published applications means loading a different page.
No presence or roster of any kind, across operators or within one.

Published applications are reached by ordinary web addresses, and the hosted service mints short permanent links for a build and for a project's primary build; there is no naming or resolution scheme for places beyond the web's own.

sources.title: PlayCanvas Hosting | PlayCanvas Developer Site
sources.quote: Builds are given permanent link in the form `https://playcanv.as/b/BUILD_ID/`.

coverage.note: No discovery of worlds, nodes or services; the hosted site lists projects for browsing, which is a catalogue, not a discovery protocol.
No shared clock or event ordering model. The runtime has only its own frame timer.
A client-side rendering runtime with no multi-user layer defines no identifier for a person, agent or thing.
No credential format, and nothing in the runtime that would consume one.
No protocol for requesting or presenting claims.
No permission grants readable by a third party. The hosted editor has project roles for developers, which is team access control, not a portable grant.
No selective disclosure, because there are no claims to disclose.
No reputation or social graph.
No licence terms are carried with an asset, so nothing can be enforced at the point of use.
Nothing expresses position or orientation against the Earth. Scene coordinates are local and unreferenced.
No coordinate reference system is named or carried; the runtime knows only its own local frame.

No user accounts and no item ownership, so there is nothing to hold or carry.
No portable settings or accessibility choices. A localisation system chooses language assets at run time, but nothing follows the user between applications.
Assets are referred to by numeric identifier and by location; nothing addresses content by hash.

The hosted editor produces a runnable package, either published to its own hosting or downloaded as a zip with an entry page and a project configuration file, and it also has a bundle asset type that groups assets into one download; the open-source runtime alone offers no packaging step, only a library on the package registry, and neither output is an interchange format anyone else reads.
